review:
This is the greatest game ever made. Insane levels of depth and is really rewarding for hardcode players. There is incredible diversity in how people approach builds. poe.ninja's ladder indexes thousands of people. Every league you can find someone high up on the ladder who is using a trash skill and finding the 3 or 4 mechanics they can combine to make it worthwhile. One thing I saw this league was lightning warp + max duration in order to run heist efficiently.

Very pro-player developers. Leagues are every 3 months and provide tons of new content, balance updates, and a fresh economy. After those 3 months, your characters and items are sent to "standard league" which is the permanent league where tons of legacy versions of items are floating around. It's an amazing way to keep things fresh and I've never quite seen a game that operates around a set schedule like this. Every new league launch PoE hits top player numbers on Steam and gets a wave of hype.

The only thing that's not great about PoE is the new player experience. As a new player you are going to have absolutely no idea what you are doing, and your build is going to suck. You'll probably have to restart in order to get a build that can finish the campaign. And most experienced PoE players consider the campaign to be like "the tutorial". Mapping is where the real game starts and opens up all of the endgame strategies and content.

review:
One of the best games ever made—if you can survive the learning cliff (700+ Hours In)

I have put over 700 hours into Path of Exile, and I am telling you straight: this is easily one of the best games I have ever played. 

Even so, my stats are kind of embarrassing—across all these seasons, I've only actually made it to the maps twice. The game is brutal! When I first started, I couldn't get past level 50 or reach Act 6 without constantly dying. I would rage quit, uninstall, leave the game for months, and then inevitably come back when a new league dropped to try again. 

And that is the beauty of PoE. Every single time I came back, I learned something new, got a bit better, and pushed a little further. The sheer depth and content of this game never get old. The build variety and complexity are unmatched, and no matter how many times it kicks my teeth in, I will always come back to check out a new league. 

Verdict: It's punishing, it has a legendary learning curve, and it will humble you—but it is an absolute masterpiece of an ARPG. Highly recommended if you love deep, endlessly rewarding progression.

review:
Pros:
* The core gameplay is great. You kill huge hordes of monsters.
* The skill gem system is cool. You can build your own skill.
* Mapping is arguably the best end game system in gaming.
* It's free! If you like it, you will want to spend like $30 on stash tab for quality-of-life.
* Great graphics, controls and production quality.
* Tons of fun content.
* Intricate and cool build options.
* The trade system is arguably the best in gaming.

Cons:
* Too many one-shot mechanics.
* The boss design is often very poor. You must learn the boss mechanics by heart, and the game doesn't teach you those mechanics.
* It is extremely imbalanced. It's not "anything goes". There are only a few "good" builds.
* Off-screening.
* There is grinding.
* Maps have become bloated with content you don't want to interact with.
* Playing standard is miserable because your build often gets nerfed and becomes obsolete. You must play league, which means you must constantly start over. Some people enjoy that. I don't enjoy it because it takes many hours (estimately at least 40) to get a character to the endgame.
* The campaign is not enjoyable. It's boring.
* There is no multiplayer. It is a single player game where you can trade with other players who also play single player.
* Melee builds are much worse than ranged. The clear speed is too low.
* Every monster in the game has stun on hit.
* In spite of much cool content, the addition of the "atlas tree" made it meaningless to interact with most of the content because it became too unrewarding.

I almost only played standard (the permanent league where you never start over). I got tired of the nerfs. The final straw for me was when they changed the rules for socket colors. Players in standard had perfect items with 6 white sockets, which required tons of investment. Then the developers suddenly reversed it and said that white sockets are now strictly worse. It felt like an insult. All my items became worse and I can't fix them because they are mirrored.

I recommend the game for its good parts, but you must play league, not standard. For most players, playing league is probably a too big time investment.

review:
I came in as someone who's been only a "casual" ARPG player. I'm a woman in my 40s, and I've been gaming ever since I got the NES I begged for Christmas in 1990. When I was in my 30s, literally 90% of my gaming focused on JRPGs. But in the past few years, I've reduced JRPGs to about 10-15% of my "gaming diet," with a lot more genre variety, including games that aren't RPGs at all.

I probably played OG Diablo and Diablo II a bit as a teenager. Earlier this year, I sunk some hours into Grim Dawn, tried some other ARPGs, and I've now got an original EXE of Diablo II: Lord of Destruction running in Wine outside of Steam, on my Linux desktop. 

I know n00bs are usally scared away from PoE due to the immense skill... not a tree, more like a series of skill forests. I followed some of the advice from PoE YouTubers, I got a loot filter right away and I started following a build guide for a melee attack optimized Scion. But after allocating several points, I realized that the build guide didn't quite align with the skill "forest" I had. I did spend the first several points on upgrading my strength. And now at level 32, I have a few nice attack traits, such as impale anf bleed.

Now that I'm navigating the skill "forest" with a lot more confidence, seeing patterns in how it's laid out while following the general advice to specialize rather than try to make my Scion a "Jill of all trades."

I'm having a lot of fun. I'm glad the Trials of Ascendancy aren't complicated puzzles, The puzzles in CrossCode were bad enough, I don't want them in my more Diablo like ARPGs. 

I'm still not sure how to be more active in my league other than to check the events board (empty for now), and play those sea maps for Valerie. When I know other players can see my character, I will likely buy a few cosmetics.

It took some fiddling to get the game to run well even though this is a mid tier gaming laptop from 2021. It's almost certainly because I'm running a version of Gentoo Linux, something I do because I'm a cybersecurity specialist and anti Gen AI political activist. 

If you have any sort of Linux distro, I strongly recommend going to ProtonDB before you launch the game for the first time and choose the version of Proton, and best launcher settings for your distro. Then, while in the game settings, switch networking (under the game tab) to either auto or predictive, never lockstep. I think I found predictive to be best. Even though my network connectivity is steady and fast, lockstep tends to lock me on the loading screen.

Once I had the right version of Proton and launcher settings (including "no logo"?), and tweaked the in-game settings a bit, with my loot filter from filterblade dot xyz manually added (adding from the filterblade web app didn't work for me, search DuckDuckGo for "Path of Exile Linux loot filter location" if you need to know where to put it in your Linux PC's file system), the game has been running great, with loading screens not lasting more than a couple of seconds and always 60 FPS or more. 

I really appreciate how Chris Wilson and the rest of GGG appear to be very pro-consumer and have no interest in Gen AI or any of that horrifying crap. 

To n00bs, don't be afraid of the skill "forest." Zoom in and out of it, and make note of the patterns of skills in it. Also keep in mind that the kind of attack or magic skills that would consume MP in a JRPG usually come from gems. Make sure to put gems in your equipment ASAP! And keep most  of the same gems through the campaign and end game, because they get more powerful and level up as you use them more.

I followed some of the advice from PoE YouTubers, I got a loot filter right away and I started following a build guide for a melee attack optimized Scion. But after allocating several points, I realized that the build guide didn't quite align with the skill "forest" I had. I did spend the first several points on upgrading my strength. Now that I'm navigating the skill "forest" with a lot more confidence, seeing patterns in how it's laid out while following the general advice to specialize rather than try to make my Scion a "Jill of all trades." I'm still not sure how to be more active in my league other than to check the events board (empty for now), and play those sea maps for Valerie. Zoom in and out of it, and make note of the patterns of skills in it. Also keep in mind that the kind of attack or magic skills that would consume MP in a JRPG usually come from gems. I did hear the complains about poe2 being too slow, but in my opinion poe1 is just too fast, 
the animations and flow of the game just starts looking messy and everything between you and the loot looses all meaning.

So i prefer the 2nd game way over the 1st.

review:
Path of Exile is an outstanding free-to-play action RPG that delivers an incredibly deep and demanding adventure through a world consumed by darkness, corruption, and supernatural horrors. Developed and published by Grinding Gear Games, it distinguishes itself through extraordinary character customization, challenging combat, and an enormous collection of interconnected progression systems. Set on the hostile continent of Wraeclast, the game places players in the role of an exile fighting to survive against terrifying creatures and powerful adversaries. Its greatest achievement is the freedom it provides to experiment with different playstyles, although that same complexity can make the experience intimidating for newcomers. For players who appreciate intricate mechanics and long-term character development, it offers one of the most substantial experiences available in the genre.

The atmosphere immediately establishes a grim and unforgiving identity. Abandoned settlements, corrupted wildernesses, ancient ruins, and grotesque monsters create a convincing world where danger feels ever-present. The narrative gradually reveals the disturbing history of Wraeclast through quests, dialogue, environmental storytelling, and encounters with memorable characters. Although the lore is extensive and fascinating, its presentation sometimes takes a secondary role to relentless combat and equipment progression. Nevertheless, the dark fantasy setting remains compelling, supported by excellent environmental design, unsettling sound effects, and atmospheric music that reinforces the feeling of exploring a civilization devastated by supernatural forces.

Combat is fast, destructive, and remarkably flexible. Players can specialize in melee attacks, ranged weapons, elemental spells, summoned allies, traps, and numerous unconventional combinations. Defeating large groups of enemies with carefully developed abilities creates an immensely satisfying sense of power, while challenging bosses demand awareness, preparation, and appropriate defensive strategies. The skill gem system is particularly impressive because abilities can be modified through support gems, allowing seemingly ordinary attacks to evolve into devastating combinations. However, encounters can become visually chaotic when numerous projectiles and effects overwhelm the screen. Certain character builds also encourage repetitive ability usage, making extended grinding sessions occasionally monotonous.

Character progression represents the game's most distinctive accomplishment. Its enormous passive skill tree provides an astonishing degree of freedom, allowing players to construct highly specialized characters without being completely restricted by traditional class identities. Ascendancy specializations introduce additional layers of customization, while equipment modifiers and skill interactions create countless opportunities for experimentation. Discovering effective combinations can be incredibly rewarding, especially when a carefully planned build begins overcoming previously impossible challenges. Unfortunately, the learning curve is exceptionally steep. Newcomers may struggle to understand complicated mechanics, and poorly distributed passive points can significantly weaken a character. The game rewards research and patience but offers comparatively little forgiveness for inexperienced decisions.

Equipment acquisition and crafting provide another compelling foundation for progression. Defeated enemies frequently drop weapons, armor, accessories, and valuable crafting materials, encouraging constant experimentation with different combinations of attributes. The unconventional currency system gives numerous resources practical crafting functions, creating a fascinating relationship between item improvement and trading. Finding a rare piece of equipment or successfully crafting a powerful upgrade can feel genuinely exciting. However, randomized outcomes occasionally make progression frustrating, particularly when substantial resources disappear without producing worthwhile improvements. Inventory management also becomes increasingly demanding as players accumulate enormous quantities of equipment and specialized materials.

The endgame offers exceptional longevity through the Atlas of Worlds, challenging maps, formidable bosses, and numerous specialized activities. Completing the main campaign opens the door to increasingly sophisticated progression systems that encourage players to refine their characters and pursue more difficult encounters. Challenge leagues further enhance replayability by introducing fresh mechanics and opportunities to begin new adventures. These features make the game particularly appealing to dedicated players who enjoy optimization and continuous improvement. However, the sheer amount of available content can feel overwhelming, and reaching the highest levels of progression often requires considerable grinding and detailed mechanical knowledge.

Multiplayer adds another dimension through cooperative encounters, trading, and community interaction. Players can collaborate against dangerous enemies or participate in an extensive economy where valuable equipment and crafting resources are exchanged. The game also supports independent progression, although a persistent internet connection remains necessary. Its free-to-play model is commendable because the core adventure and substantial endgame content are accessible without mandatory purchases. Most optional transactions involve cosmetics, while additional stash tabs provide meaningful storage convenience. These purchases are not required to enjoy the campaign, but dedicated players may find them increasingly useful.

From a technical perspective, the game delivers impressive environmental detail, distinctive monster designs, and spectacular combat effects. Its visual presentation successfully captures the brutality of its setting, although performance can fluctuate during encounters involving numerous enemies and elaborate abilities. Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable, meaning the game can be enjoyed on Valve's handheld system but is not fully Verified. Controller support makes combat accessible, although navigating complicated menus, managing inventory, and examining detailed equipment descriptions can feel cumbersome on the smaller display. Graphically demanding encounters may also require reduced settings for smoother performance.

Ultimately, Path of Exile is a remarkable achievement in action RPG design, offering exceptional customization, rewarding combat, and almost overwhelming replayability. Its greatest weaknesses are its intimidating complexity, occasional performance problems, demanding inventory management, and reliance on repetitive grinding. Nevertheless, these shortcomings rarely diminish the satisfaction of mastering its elaborate systems and developing increasingly powerful characters. It is particularly recommended for players who enjoy strategic character building, challenging encounters, and extensive endgame progression. Those seeking a casual adventure may find its demands exhausting, but dedicated enthusiasts will discover an extraordinarily rewarding experience. 

Rating: 9/10

review:
[H1]So what's it about?[/H1]
In POE you are a criminal sentenced to death but instead shipped to the cursed continent of Wraeclast. You start with nothing and end up fighting Gods and other divine being. But to get there you will go through many beautifully crafted levels with many systems. At first it is intimidating and for your first run I highly recommend using a guide from for example [url=https://mobalytics.gg/poe/builds] Mobalytics [/url].

POE is an older game but can be measured against new releases as it has received and continues to receive updated. I've been an avid fan of Diablo and Diablo 2 since they were released (I was one of the first in D2 in Europe to hit lvl 99 back in the day). D3 was OK but not what I was looking into an ARPG and I've avoided D4 ever since the "don't you have phones" and all of the monetization; it's clear the Blizzard of old is no longer there.

POE is F2P but it doesn't mean P2W. Every couple of months new supporter packs are released that are time limited. But they are just cosmetics and the game comes with plenty. Only buy those if you want to support the developers. At most you probably spend about £30 to make your life easier with more inventory tabs but only gets those after you've played the game for a while and it's still not required for the first play through but it will help a lot managing all the loot you collect later on. Consider the campaign the trial or demo version to see if the game is for you.

You pick one of the available 7 classes when you start the game. As you progress you can then further specialise the class in the direction you like. There is so much to choose from that it will keep you busy for a long time. 

The campaign has 10 acts and those are really just the tutorial to avoid overloading you with the many systems POE has. After that the real game begins and it's all about completing maps at an increased difficulty for better rewards. Following that you arrive at the real end-game. It's a big game for sure :-).

It's great solo but multiplayer is good too. There is even PVP if you're interested in that. 

[H1]The good[/H1]
It has the most extensive systems I have ever seen in any ARPG. Just the skill tree alone is massive. This allows for a lot of experimentation to find the ideal setup. Your class is just a starting point and you can adjust how you feel fit.

I love the voice acting, the enemies and the graphical effects; GGG voice actors and artists are some of the best in class. 

There are many different leagues you can play (comparable to seasons in other games), including hard core and you can build even your own if you feel like.

The developers play their game and there are frequent updates. Tournaments are organised and if you watch them on Twitch you even get nice stuff from time to time.

The inner loot goblin is always satisfied when doing one of the many side activities in game. There is so much to collect and there is a variation of activities to keep it all fresh. 

You have your own hideout that you can decorate as you please. Later this becomes your central hub.

There is in-game trading with other players and multiplayer is supported. There is also a [url= https://www.pathofexile.com/trade ]trade post [/url] where you can buy and sell items you want or find.
The game plays really fast at times - much higher speed than D2; which is great it’s a constant adrenaline rush. The drawback is if your build has a weakness there is little room for error on the high end levels as it leaves you with little time to counter act.

[H1]The not so good[/H1]
There is definitely a deep learning curve hence I advise using a guide for the first play through so you get an understanding of the basics. 

End game (lvl 90 - 100) can be really challenging depending on your build. Some require expensive (as in rare items they are player trade) to be effective and the AI will relentlessly punish you if you have a weak build to the point you want to give up. 

To counter this you probably want to start with a character that is less depended on gear and more on skills which are easier to come by. A second build could be one that is more depending on gear as you can use the first character to farm where necessary. In general: ranged class / skills are easier than melee especially later in the game.

For every new character you create you need to go through all 10 acts of the campaign; thankfully because of the stash, your hideout and all the other different game modes, including the progress in the second part (Atlas) is account wide it's not a major issue but it would be better if you would be given the option to skip the whole campaign after the first time that you've completed it (similar to like GW2 for example).

I disapprove of the lootbox mechanic introduced every season. It's not required, it's not in your face but it can cause serious issues for people that are vulnerable to gambling addiction. The positive maybe is that all the loot from the loot boxes are released later in the MTX store but still it should not be in the game.

[H1]The DLCs[/H1]
There are no DLCs other than supporter packs that only add cosmetics to the game. There is a microtransactions (MTX) store to buy cosmetics and QoL items. If you want to get any of those wishlist them and wait for a sale (every couple of weeks). Note that some of the MTX from POE is compatible with POE2 in particular most of the inventory tabs. 

[H1]Summary[/H1]
The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, the second best time is now. This is true for POE. I wish I had discovered it earlier but I'm happy I did eventually. If you're into ARPG it's one of the best games to get. Highly recommended.

review:
5000小时，n个赛季40挑战全通，n个10镜+角色的体验：糟糕至极。

(1）游戏纯纯为了不让玩家无敌通关设计，只管难，不管平衡，完全毁灭了角色扮演的本质：构筑一个角色从0开始慢慢变无敌。
用暗黑2举例，你无论选任何角色，只要靠肝都可以变得无敌通关，也都能打uber。poe恰恰相反，你无论选任何角色，哪怕用最op的bd，他也保证你有内容打不过:
自伤bd禁疗内容(emzebeler罪魂瓦尔多，uber maven 85贤主)一秒自杀打不了
瓦尔多2m远程没法打
瓦尔多罪魂百亢一击线低于150k物理300k元素没法打
瓦尔多罪魂百亢脱装-环效dps少于10亿根本不掉血
t16.5/t17 100deli多词条混沌伤(-30抗性/as extra chaos/wither)血流派都没法打即使3万血
深矿ehp低于500k没法打，dps低于1e没法打
综合一下要全通的角色需要10亿dps，走es ci，ehp500k+，元素一击300k+这样的角色赛季根本不存在。而这要求仅仅是能打，即是6门有比较大概率能过，不代表不死，甚至不代表6门一定通。
更别提终局平衡跟狗屎一样，你要强力的bd只能在以下选：t0 18耐力球ci勇士，护甲人，影陨卫士，t1 千力勇士，佣兵。这里面4/5近战，而且一共就这几个选项其他都是垃圾。你选了其他这游戏会变得奇难无比，你只能这也不打那也不打发挥阿q精神觉得自己很强。
arpg最重要的是rpg角色扮演，你今天游戏平衡狗屎一样的逼人只能玩某些他不喜欢的bd角色扮演在哪里？我是正好是近战爱好者，可是如果有个玩家他只喜欢玩弓手呢？他必须接受死的跟傻逼一样？稍微难一点的图就6门死光？

(2)装备太稀有，导致极大不公平
装备越稀有，价值越高，高到一定程度任何玩家通过努力肝都无法获得只能靠欧或者rmt导致游戏极度不公平。比如3.28赛季的双神龛腰带(加速/抗性，回响/抗性这些都是10镜起)，你要吗自己欧出来要吗rmt。人家欧一下10个镜子顶你核心玩家一赛季收益，普通玩家10赛季收益，这还怎么玩？你整个赛季肝几百小时就买人家欧一下。

review: This game is nothing short of an absolute masterpiece. I first came to know half life back in 2024 when one of my friends mentioned it because we were playing Gmod and he spawned the buggy from later chapters of the game (yes ik i was playing gmod and didnt even know what half life was lol) This then caused me to look at the steam page for half life 2, think its cool, and wishlist it, never to be seen again (until it was). Then, while looking through my emails, i found one from steam stating that half life 2 was on sale. At the time I didn't have a good relationship with my friends, I was always trying to fit in and do what I thought made me look the "coolest" in their eyes. And so, in an effort to relate to them, I bought the game, played it for about 30 min, loved it, and went to go tell my friends, you wanna know what they said? "ok" and "cool" that was it. From that moment on I realized that nobody actually cares what I do, they pretend to dislike you for not doing something, and then when you do that thing they care even less. So you wanna know what I did? i played half life 2, i beat half life 2, then i played half life 1, then i played half life 2 in vr, then episode 1, then episode 1 in vr, and then episode 2 in vr, and then i spent hours and hours watching half life args, mod vids, funny clips, short films, theories, becoming so obsessed with the game i would fall asleep every night listening to city 17 ambience. I'm even in the process of building my own fully functioning bullet resistant HEV suit, and all that I can say is, half life (as a series) is the greatest piece of media to ever grace this amazing planet. Half life taught me how to keep going when it's hard, how to do hard things simply because others might benefit, and most importantly, how to love myself when no one else does. After playing half life 2 I became openly a furry, and openly Bi, and i didnt care, i didnt care who thought what anymore, sure i lost some friends, but if i lost them because i became my true self, then were they ever my friends in the first place? If you take anything from this review, (other than of course playing half life lol) it's that the only person that has an opinion that actually matters is you, pay no attention to all the people that think you can't do it, be like Gordon, and do it anyway. Thank you, Half Life and VALVe.

review:
**Not every classic holds up in 2026.**

I understand how revolutionary Half-Life 2 must have been back in 2004, but playing it for the first time today has been a letdown.

The shooting got repetitive pretty quickly, and the story never really grabbed me. I kept waiting for that moment when everything would click and I'd understand why people call this one of the greatest games ever, but it just never happened.

It's not like I hate old games. I've enjoyed plenty of them, but this one felt like a chore to play. I eventually dropped it because I wasn't having fun anymore.

A little advice for new players: Don't go into this expecting one of the greatest FPS experiences ever just because of its legendary reputation. If you're playing it for the first time in 2026, remember that what was revolutionary back then might not feel so special today. You might love it, but keep your expectations in check.

Though I can still respect its historical impact without enjoying the game myself.

review:
[h1]Why Half-Life 2 Is an Uncontested Masterpiece[/h1]

I have completed the entire Half life game series(The Orange Box) upwards of 35 times across several different systems that I've had in the past. In fact, I’ve unlocked every single achievement across the entire saga, searching every hidden corner to wring out every last piece of lore and mechanical genius Valve packed into it. Yet, even after decades of evolving graphics, massive open worlds, and complex mechanics, this 2004 titan remains the undisputed gold standard of narrative first-person shooters. It earns the title of a true masterpiece not through flashy gimmicks, but because every single element. Its revolutionary physics, flawless pacing, world-building, and player agency works in absolute, unbroken harmony. For me, it isn't just nostalgia talking... Half-Life 2 holds a deeply special place in my heart over the years because of how effortlessly it blends physics-driven gameplay with an unforgettable storyline.

[h2]Physics, Pacing, and Pure Innovation[/h2]
What elevates Half-Life 2 to masterpiece status mechanically is its incredible design language. The Source engine didn't just render City 17, it made the world tangible. The iconic Gravity Gun wasn't just a clever weapon, it transformed the entire environment into a canvas for creative problem-solving.

Whether you're flinging saw blades through Ravenholm, clearing Combine barricades, or solving environmental physics puzzles, the gameplay feels tactile, responsive, and infinitely satisfying. The pacing is a masterclass in variety, one moment you're navigating high-tension horror scenarios, the next you're speeding across coastal highway stretches on the Highway 17 buggy or leading an antlion swarm into battle.

[h2]Immersive World-Building and Unmatched Lore[/h2]
Beyond the mechanics, the narrative structure proves why the game is an artistic triumph. Valve famously avoids traditional cutscenes and jarring info-dumps. Instead, you experience every single moment through the eyes of Gordon Freeman, making you an active participant in the story rather than a passive observer.

The lore surrounding humanity’s subjugation under the totalitarian, interdimensional Combine is delivered with incredible subtlety and weight:
[list]
[*]The chilling, hollow announcements echoing through City 17.

[*]The dystopian surveillance and bleak, industrial architecture swallowing human history.

[*]Unforgettable companions like Alyx Vance, whose genuine emotional grounding and smart AI design set a benchmark for companion characters that few games have matched since.
[list]
The overarching mystery of the Combine, the enigma of the G-Man, and the silent resilience of the human resistance build an unmatched sense of scale and intriguing environment. 

[h2]Final Verdict[/h2]
Half-Life 2 isn't just a great game, it is a timeless monument in gaming history that fundamentally changed how video games tell stories and handle world interactivity. Having earned every achievement and played through the saga dozens of times across different generations of hardware, my appreciation for its brilliant world, revolutionary mechanics, and incredible narrative only continues to grow. It is, without a doubt, gaming at its absolute peak.

Half-Life 2 is an absolute legendary game and easily one of the greatest video games ever made. With an incredible story, unforgettable atmosphere, revolutionary mechanics, and groundbreaking physics, this game set new standards for the entire gaming industry.

The story of Gordon Freeman and his fight against the Combine is absolutely fantastic. The world-building, memorable characters, mysterious atmosphere, and incredible storytelling keep you hooked from beginning to end. The story is filled with intense moments, unexpected twists, and amazing cliffhangers that leave you wanting more.

The gameplay mechanics are simply outstanding, especially considering when the game was released. The movement feels great, the gunplay is satisfying, and the physics system was nothing short of revolutionary. The Gravity Gun alone is one of the greatest weapons ever introduced in a video game, making combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving incredibly fun and creative.

The level design is phenomenal, offering a perfect mix of action, exploration, puzzles, and unforgettable sequences. From the streets of City 17 to the terrifying atmosphere of Ravenholm, every location feels unique and memorable.

Even after all these years, Half-Life 2 still holds up incredibly well. Its incredible physics, immersive storytelling, and brilliant gameplay are a testament to just how far ahead of its time this game truly was.

Overall, an absolute masterpiece that revolutionized gaming and influenced countless games that followed. One of the greatest games ever created, and personally, my favorite video game of all time. Nothing comes close to the experience Half-Life 2 delivers. A legendary achievement by Valve and an easy 11/10!

review:
When the original Half-Life was released it completely changed the genre forever.   It showed that a FPS didn't have to just be a run and gun shooter in 3D.   You could have a film like story and narrative, with acting and events.   You were in a story that progressed with you.  And with the Source remake it's worth playing again,

Half-Life 2 took this to another level of immersion.  You really felt like you were in the game world, and not just trying to reach the end of a level.    It has so many memorable set pieces and events.   I've played through the whole game multiple times and still smile every time I reach certain points.   The prison section being one of my favourites. 

Most games released in 2004 looks very dated these days.  Blocky primitive 3D objects and characters, low resolution textures.   But somehow Half-Life 2 still looks as great as it did the day it was released.    And the updates Valve made to the game for the Steam Deck release just shows how the developers never abandon their games.   They are made with a passion and supported forever where possible.    I replayed though the whole game again on the Steam Deck and it was just as great, if not even better thanks to the Gyro aiming, which really adds a new level of control to any FPS.

This is not just IMO the greatest First Person Shooter ever created, but one of the greatest games ever made.

review:
Half-Life 2...

The game still is very good, even all these years after its release. 
The world is full of life, the sound design and music are phenomenal, and the PHYSICS are something I still don’t see in today’s most modern games. It’s fun, it has an incredible lore, and I completely understand why people call it one of the best games ever made. If it’s still this good today, I can’t imagine how revolutionary it must have felt to play back then.

One of the things I appreciate most, besides the physics, is the “chase scenes.” They’re common in games: you hop into a vehicle and have to drive, either to escape or to chase an enemy. Until Half-Life, I always said I didn’t like them. They felt forced, and even though I was the one driving, it seemed like the game was just telling me where to go. But Half-Life completely changed how I see scenes like these. The driving is so good, satisfying, and freeing that I ended up loving every moment behind the wheel.

And nobody can take away the joy I felt every time I lost all my items and finally got the gravity gun back. It’s incredible how much fun simple mechanics can be when they’re well implemented.

I absolutely recommend Half-Life 2.
Here’s a phenomenal quote that sums up the whole experience of the game:

“The right man in the wrong place can make all the difference in the world.”

review:
对于没有3d眩晕问题的玩家，绝对是款不可错过的好游戏。
所有美好体验的前提是不要看攻略，探路解密的设计非常出色：
诚然相比于在2026年很多引导都做成宝宝巴士的3a大作，半条命2的引导已经很“hard”了，但这正是一大乐趣所在，全程充满着“我试一下能不能成”的心态找出答案所反馈的惊喜。
虽然存在少数需要对上电波的解密，个人觉得整体难度尚可，只要稍有耐心多尝试下不同思路就不会卡关。

对比1代的体验，最大的感受是不再孤单压抑：
归功于引擎画面的提升和脚本演出的打磨，半条命2的叙事演出放在今天依然出色。v社将重力枪和ai队友的设计发挥的淋漓尽致，这些游戏早期就见识到的核心功能，到了后期仍然不会感到无聊，随着流程推进不断出现的新物品和新敌人相得益彰，配合着新地图总是能玩出花样。

review:
不想吹毛求疵，21年前的游戏在关卡解密、地图设计和物理引擎做的相当成熟，完全不输现在的游戏。但以现代眼光来看确实存在不少缺点，画质难免较差、老游戏部分机制落后、手感过分轻飘以及存在很多BUG。

战斗方面，对敌手段相当丰富，有各种武器和交互用来对策各种类型敌人。一些章节还可以用载具、固定机枪和指挥宝可梦蚁狮应敌。

剧情方面，世界观很庞大，但对没玩过前作的不太友好，不看解析完全理不清各方势力和主要角色错综复杂的关系，主线里很多前情和设定是真一点不给交代。全流程下来无论走到哪都被友军当成救世主，有种“天下谁人不识君”的感觉，代入感和情绪价值给得相当足。

虽说老游戏蹩脚的的地方不少，但本体和两个DLC全流程下来还是有些意犹未尽，有生之年期待能有3代或者半条命Alyx那样的重制版吧。

review:
1. FPS 发展史的教科书，当年直接重新定义线性叙事射击，没有强制播片，全程保持玩家第一人称沉浸感。
2. 重力枪是游戏设计的神来之笔，利用物理环境解谜杀敌，这个玩法放到 20 多年后依旧新鲜感十足。
3. 17 号城的压迫氛围塑造无敌，联合军占领下的压抑末世，配乐、路人台词、环境细节全部服务世界观。
4. 莱温霍姆小镇永远是经典名场面，紧张恐怖感拉满，神父这个 NPC 塑造至今很难超越。
5. 汽船 / 越野车长途驾驶段落争议很大，喜欢的觉得沉浸，讨厌的觉得重复跑路，节奏拖沓枯燥。
6. 老游戏枪械手感偏厚重，没有现代 FPS 顺滑的反馈，习惯 COD、泰坦陨落的玩家上手会不习惯。
7. 20 周年更新自带优质中文语音，配音水准很高，重温体验提升巨大，对国内玩家非常友好。
8. 创意工坊 MOD 生态极其繁荣，无数民间重制、剧情 MOD，通关本体之后还能玩大量衍生内容。
9. 敌人 AI 有年代局限，有时行为比较僵硬，怪物种类不算多，战斗模式后期略有重复。
10. 结局戛然而止，故事并未完结，一定要连着 EP1、EP2 一起玩；只玩本体的话会卡在悬念处意难平。

review:
《半衰期 2》毫无疑问在玩法创意，画面质量，引导水平三个方面做到的那个年代的顶尖水准。有些方面甚至是革命性的。
作为起源引擎的首秀，展现出了惊为天人的可交互性，即使在现代，拥有这种交互性单人FPS游戏也不多见。无论是地上的罐子或者木箱，游戏绝大部分物件玩家都可以捡起来或者移动，并且对npc或者玩家有碰撞反应。拥有重力枪时，可以重力枪吸起附近的物件射出去击杀敌人，或者把一些物件吸过来当跳板进行解谜。非常有趣味性。
在引导方面，不像一些现代游戏，往物件上涂上黄色油漆告诉你这有路可走。而是通过坏境的引导。我印象深刻的一个解谜应该是第二章的一段，应该是类似于滑轮的谜题，你需要把上面的洗衣机推下去让电梯拉不上去，从而搭建出一个跳板。这种引导，解谜在游戏中还有很多，但是来的基本恰到好处，V社对节奏把控的很好。这样的解谜不难，但又能给玩家足够的满足感。连我一个非常厌恶解谜的人都玩的很享受，基本没卡过几次关。
音乐也是顶中顶，好听而且非常契合战斗场景，更加战斗爽。
总结：12/10，必玩之作。即使在2026年的今天，它的gameplay依旧丝毫不过时。
现在真希望我有一台VR设备去玩alyx。

review:
放两年前我刚玩完那会儿评价，肯定开口就是“神作！此生必玩系列！”
但这两年看过很多人的负面评价“操作难受，晕3d”“引导弱”“流程太长”“难度太大”“手感一般”后，我就知道，半条命2注定只在我这里是一部好作品了。
毕竟1000个人眼里有1000个哈姆雷特，没有什么游戏是所有人都喜欢的，即便是这种被玩家圈里公认的好作品。
（P.S.沟槽的v社为什么把半条命整合了呀，搞的当时我原本打的全成就没了，最后只能通过下载第一章和第二章然后重新导入成就，所以这也是为什么我成就都是基本同一个时间开的，你们要看可以去看我库里那个半条命2第一章和半条命2第二章的成就，这个现在已经被v社归类到插件类和半条命2合并了，但当时是游戏，我就是分着下载玩的。）
虽然有以上种种，但并不妨碍这部作品在我这里的地位。
他帮我度过了我大学低配电脑那些年的窘迫和无味。那时候看着库里买的2077，战地1和底特律变人等等大作但是带不动，很是悲哀。
直到有天看到了半条命，买了橙色包后一发不可收拾，把这一整个系列都玩完了，而且还特意买了橙色包没包含的蓝色沸点和针锋相对这两部。
我感觉这个系列的游戏很对我胃口，不管是地图设计，武器手感，还有一代移动时轻微的晃动感，感觉太舒服了，除了画质和建模，给我的感觉不像是个二十多年前的游戏。
尤其是第二部，可以说对比一代是巨大的提升，武器丰富，玩法创新，角色ai比早期高级了好几个档次。当时在宿舍里玩的废寝忘食，打到进入联军控制塔后本来以为游戏都结束了，结果还有老长一段，给我整的激动的，差点熬夜。
以及那个不用枪械通关莱温霍姆的成就，很多时候极限操作给我玩的头皮发麻，那个场景和怪物的设计给人很强的压迫感，玩的时候感觉那些子爬墙的红色怪能爬出电脑给我吃了。
还有2结局重返城里集结那些流浪的反抗军然后带着小队跟联军对抗真的沉浸感拉满，在废墟下面躲三脚架机器时给我的恐惧感一直到后来玩死亡空间都没有再出现。
还有海边开车冲破一个个关卡，以及监狱里边操纵沙蚁边绕迷宫都让我印象深刻。算是我玩完后为数不多能每个环节都让我记忆犹新的游戏了，希望你在很多游戏都做不到，玩完就忘了。
我还给我弟安利，他也还好，玩到监狱末尾那一段，但后来也放弃了，果然这游戏还是不太适合现在。
如果现在让我评价他，那我绝对会说这是我steam上迄今为止买过最不亏的游戏。

review:
[h1]Sixteen Years Later, Still Setting the Standard[/h1]

After more than [b]530 hours[/b] with Civilization V, I still consider it one of the finest 4X strategy games ever made. Its enduring appeal lies not in any single mechanic, but in how successfully its systems work together.

[b]For me, Civilization has always been about building an empire, not simply conquering one.[/b] Developing a prosperous economy, advancing technology, managing diplomacy, and preparing for occasional wars all contribute to a satisfying sense of historical progression. Civilization V strikes an exceptional balance between these competing priorities. Every decision feels connected to the civilization you are creating.

It is certainly not without flaws. Diplomatic behavior can be inconsistent, the AI occasionally makes questionable military decisions, and the late game can become tedious. Yet these shortcomings rarely undermine the strength of the overall experience, particularly with the Gods & Kings and Brave New World expansions.

[u][b]Civilization V versus Civilization VII[/b][/u]

Civilization VII deserves credit for attempting to reinvent aspects of the series. However, its changes to empire development create a fundamentally different experience. Where Civilization V emphasizes the continuity of guiding one civilization through history, Civilization VII places greater emphasis on adaptation and reinvention between eras.

[i]Neither philosophy is inherently wrong, but I find Civilization V's approach considerably more satisfying.[/i]

Sixteen years after release, Civilization V continues to receive remarkably positive recent Steam reviews. This speaks volumes about the enduring satisfaction players find in its design.

[b]Civilization V succeeds because it understands something fundamental: the greatest pleasure of a 4X strategy game is watching an empire develop through decisions that remain meaningful from the first turn to the last.[/b]

[u][b]Verdict: Highly Recommended.[/b][/u]

[i]Some games age. Others endure. Civilization V has earned its place among the latter.[/i]

Rating: 10 / 10

I can't have 1K+ hours in this game and not give it a 10 / 10.  Is it actually a 10 / 10?  I don't know, but I became so used to this game that when I tried Civ 6, I instantly hated it... everything was different, and I guess I got lumped in with the other mouth breathers that love 5.

This game has so much to offer, and for some reason, the progression from barbs to high class nuking society never got old.  The unique perks for each civ were fun to explore.  The automation of your workers is god level design, and you can't convince me otherwise Civ 6ers.

I will say that the enemy's naval units seems busted... as in actually busted, not in a good way; they're pretty stupid, even on Deity.  Speaking of the Deity difficulty, screw you Firaxis... you people are evil... just straight up letting the CPU cheat is so unfair and obviously difficult.

Achievement-wise, double screw you Firaxis.  Some of those Deity achievements were absolutely insane.  The only way to win was pure luck + a Beautiful Mind calculated moves down to the last turn.  I save scummed the Praise the Victories one until I won at turn 99 (of 100), and an embarrassing amount of time dedicated to that 1 achievement.  You don't feel a sense of accomplishment from it because you have to save scum to win, and that never feels great.  Other notable awful ones... Pax Romana, Red Badge of Courage, and some of those Into the Renaissance achievements.

Having said all that, it's so much fun getting to a level of experience in this game where you bully the CPU... set up a game where you can only win by domination, getting nuclear subs before the CPU on a water map, and then they eventually all turn on you at the same time and fighting them off.  Buncha babies, I got nukes, what you got?  OH YOUR STUPID PLANES/MILITARY THAT YOU PULL OUT OF THIN AIR?  Whatever, I'm over it.

I realize most of my reviews are anecdotal and scatterbrained, so you're going to have to deal with it, and take my word for it bro... this game is absolutely worth it, and sooooo much better than Civ 6.

review: Hands down the best Civ entry and that's kind of painful to write in 2026 when we have two newer entries, but it's a fact. This was the entry that started the hex based single unit phase and it was an amazing change. War felt strategic where in previous entries you'd just throw doomstacks back and forth. This is also the last time the game actually focused on the Civilizations. Civilization 6 and 7 leaned way to hard into historical leaders. Building cities and developing your lands was also peak with this game. 6 spilled the cities out onto the map which made no sense since we've only urbanized about 3% of available land on Earth even today. That and they went crazy with adjacency bonuses in 6 and made them even worse in 7. They don't feel like civilization anymore, they feel more like a dorfromantic style map puzzler. Until a different team of developers gets to make a new entry, or a true competitor comes out of nowhere the way Cities Skylines knocked out Sim City, this is the turn based historical sim you're looking for.

review:
Most of the people giving this game a thumbs-up probably don't even play it anymore. A lot of the positive opinions seem to come from nostalgia or a few flashy gameplay moments. But if you actually play the game seriously, you quickly realize how many frustrating mechanics it has.

Here are just a few examples:

* **Advanced-tech wars:** The moment you reach the advanced tech era, suddenly BARBAR TANKS or BARBAR SAM launchers start spawning out of literally nowhere. No warning, no reasonable explanation — they just appear because the game wants to punish you. You can be rich, powerful, and well-prepared, and the game basically says: *"Oh, you're doing well? Let's make your gameplay poor and bad because we can."*

* **DLC multiplayer:** The game is so badly designed that if YOU own a DLC but your friend doesn't, your friend can't properly join/play with you. It's basically the game saying: *"Your friend doesn't have the DLC? Too bad. Go play something else with your broke buddy."* 

So yeah, nostalgia can make people remember this game fondly, but nostalgia doesn't magically make bad mechanics good.

If you're looking for a strategy game, there are plenty of better options. **Don't play this just because people remember it fondly.**

review:
Honestly, I didn't expect to enjoy this entry as much as I did.
Coming from Civ 5, I initially found the art style, character designs, and UI a bit off-putting, especially considering how charming Civ 5's presentation was. However, they gradually grow on you, and the game starts to feel more beginner-friendly, with each branch of progression,Units,buildingsmechanics being relatively easier to identify and navigate.
There are also more varied interactions and unique mechanics for each civilization, which was one of my biggest complaints about Civ 5. On top of that, you have more unique actions available for different units and buildings or Civ, which helps break up the tedious cycle of "press next turn until you can actually do something."
What I appreciate the most, though, are the quotes that accompany technology unlocks. They feel much more noticeable and memorable than they did in Civ 5. But the music felt a bit on the weaker side maybe i was not paying attention to it as much. The game rules and modifiers are also a welcome addition, as they introduce some much-needed chaos and variety.

The most annoying mechanic I've encountered so far is the World Council, which becomes available quite early but has barely any noticeable impact until around the midgame and the global warming mechanic with the floods but the natural disasters and zombies are quite funny. The map generation also feels somewhat lacking but as usual, mods can fix most of these complaints, and some of them introduce much-desired QoL improvements. I hope the developers take note and implement some of these features in their future games. It seems to be a recurring pattern where they overlook certain UI elements or fail to provide enough context on how particular mechanics are can to work.

review:
What I love most about Civ VI is the amount of control and meaningful decisions it gives me. I enjoy expanding aggressively in the early game, securing territory, building defensible borders and preparing for potential wars. Then comes my favorite part: developing those settlements into powerful, specialized cities while carefully balancing food, production, gold, science and culture.

Managing builders, assigning citizens to specific tiles, planning districts and optimizing individual cities might seem like unnecessary micromanagement to some, but to me, that's the heart of Civilization. Every little decision contributes to something bigger. You're not just watching an empire grow; you're building it yourself. The real enjoyment comes from developing an empire and competing with other civilizations throughout history.

Civ VI wasn't perfect at launch. I initially found its art style a little goofy, and I believe some of the content introduced through expansions should have been part of the base game. I'm not a fan of games relying on paid DLC to feel complete. However, Rise and Fall and Gathering Storm helped turn an already enjoyable game into something truly exceptional.

Playing Civilization VII has actually made me appreciate Civ VI even more. While VII introduces some interesting ideas, I feel that too many meaningful decisions have been simplified, automated or removed entirely. Losing builders, manual tile management and much of the freedom I had when developing my empire has reminded me why I enjoyed the previous games so much.

I don't need a Civilization game to be more complicated just for the sake of complexity. I want the freedom to make meaningful decisions and experience the consequences of those decisions throughout thousands of years of history. 

That's what Civilization VI does so well!!
It's not about winning as quickly as possible. It's about taking a single settler, founding a civilization, shaping its history and eventually looking across the map at an empire that exists because of the choices you made.

Civilization VI isn't perfect, but it's a fantastic strategy game, and one I can happily spend another thousand hours playing.

review:
Even ten years later, core conflicts in the game are not fixed. Diplomacy is entirely useless and the best way to do it is just to ignore it entirely. Districts and wonders taking up entire tiles breaks your ability to play tall or on islands. 

This seems like a minor problem, but it is particularly egregious when you consider that they made poorly planned choices such as Kupe; He is an oceanic-spawning leader that is typically found on small islands, whose ability requires leaving nature untouched. In previous games where your city only took up one tile, this was possible. But with the way that Civ 6 works, his ability works directly against itself and the mechanics of the game. 

Diplomacy just straight up doesn't work. The game will ignore it's own systems, and it does not track very basic concepts like "you have to survive to win the game". The AI will literally refuse to hand over diplomatic favour points in order to keep playing, and choose instead to die.

The AI for units also doesn't exist. They just wander about randomly on their own, there is absolutely no central command script, and they are useless. If you ever wonder why the enemy infantry gets in the way of their own siege units from reaching your city, it's because they literally are not co-ordinated in any way.

There are so many of these issues in the game, it's clear that nobody was talking to each other when they made it. On their own they sound like okay ideas, but put together they make each other actively worse.

review:
我的评价是：不如5代。
对于种田流玩家极度不友好，几乎逼着玩家尽快进入战争模式，尽快与AI交战。
先说发展：
同样的发展速度，同样的扩张速度，AI就是要比玩家发展得快，而且快很多。玩家还是中世纪时，就已经有AI发展到了原子时代。
更要命的是，蛮族的发展也要快于玩家，甚至能依靠先进的军事单位攻陷玩家的城池。玩家如果不开风灵月影，几乎需要五十个回合才能追平AI的发展速度。
再说外交：
AI对玩家总是怀有深深的恶意，横挑鼻子竖挑眼。玩家军事能力弱的时候，个个都看不起，甚至会集体无端宣战，然后就一直拖着不和解。
可问题是，玩家与AI的交战，往往会被那些未交战状态的AI视为好战狂。这是什么逻辑？战争是AI挑起的，回头怪玩家过于暴力。
而且这些AI都表现得特别愣，要么宣战以后，稍微攻击他们的城池，他们立刻就请求和解。要么就死硬到底，哪怕丢城失地也不肯和解。
所以AI总是趋于调和的，你跟他们说：我占了你们的城池，投降吧。他们不肯。你用核弹洗地，他们就愿意和解了，甚至割城献地。
本作的战争几乎完全围绕制空权展开，地面部队完全成了摆设。只需要大力兴建机场和空中单位，就能瘫痪一个国家的陆军。地面仅需要维持快速机动兵力（直升机、坦克）占城即可。
五代那种防空车锁区的优势，再也不复存在。防空车只保护伴随的地面单位，而且十防九空，三架战斗机就能报销一辆防空车，自身无一损伤。
地面部队拉到边境，几乎完全成了靶子。只需要几个回合，就能将玩家辛辛苦苦培养的三星地面部队全部报销。
即使有了战斗机也无法形成空中优势，需要海量的战斗机巡航制空，才能避免空军单位损失。
最后再说操作：
可以说极其繁琐。
科研和行政拉到顶后，依然需要时不时勾选，就一个选项了，有什么好选的，不能循环吗？
本作的AI占地逻辑极为愚蠢，城池建得极为密集。西安的郊外就是北京。我的好邻居图拉真，就接壤的一小块地，也要挤进去建一座城，真是有毛病啊。
部分建筑需要建在城外空地的设计，也是让人一头雾水，也就是说，每一座城，我都要算好哪些建筑要摆在郊外，然后规划用地。不能像五代那样，全都建在城里。
最后的话：
我算是模拟经营游戏的爱好者，文明五代和群星之类的游戏也没少玩。本作给我的感觉就是，不管你做什么，都比AI慢，不管你做什么，都有AI在骂。
整个游戏环境就跟火影村一样，玩家弱小的时候被霸凌，玩家强大了还是会被霸凌，霸之意志发作了属于是。
在其他游戏里，努力就会有回报。发展早，发展快，就是可以形成代差，就是可以欺凌弱小的国家。但在本作里，你发展得快（几乎不可能），AI会骂你。你发展得慢，AI就会对你宣战，然后骂你是战争狂。几乎找不到任何乐趣。

review:
By the 100-hour mark, I have successfully reached the epilogue and completed most of the NPC questlines. I am now going for 100% achievements. This is one of the first games I have ever purchased on Steam. Supergiant did a great job with the music and voice acting, especially their portrayal of Hades and the love he has for his wife.

I love the core roguelike mechanics, where each run feels unique and different boon combinations lead to completely different outcomes. Even after 100 hours, there are still many things I haven't tried, such as the other weapons. I finished the main story and epilogue using only the sword, so I am excited to explore the rest of the arsenal. The Heat system keeps the game addictive long after unlocking the main achievements, making it a game with endless replay value.

My personal favorite characters are Artemis, Nyx, and Dionysus. They are always a highlight whenever I encounter them during a run.

The world design across the different regions (Tartarus, Asphodel, Elysium, Greece, and the Temple of Styx) is distinct and visually striking. Seeing Greece for the first time after defeating the final boss was picturesque.

The main boss fight in Elysium was a bit frustrating on initial runs, but it eventually became fun. On the other hand, the main boss of Asphodel felt a bit too easy, even on my first playthrough.

While the game offers a God Mode if the learning curve feels too steep, I recommend experiencing it on the default difficulty.

As for characters I did not connect with as much, Ares stands out. I usually avoid his boons and pick other options instead.

I completed my first five successful runs using a keyboard and mouse, but I switched to a controller after getting one. The story progression feels smooth, making it easy to play for 2 to 3 hours in a single session. It is one of the few games where I do not even keep background yt videos or podcasts playing while I play.

I have not bought the sequel yet, as I want to get 100% achievements on this one first, but I cannot wait to play Hades 2. I would easily recommend this game to any fan of Greek mythology.

review:
Upon writing this review, I've almost clocked in 72 hours hours in this game, I've completed the main story, and I'm still working towards 100% completion. And honestly? I'm still not tired of it.

I love everything about this game. The dialogues, the story progression, the character development, the way every character feels like an actual person with their own personality and history. The way the story unfolds naturally as you keep playing, even when you're dying over and over again, is just brilliant. You don't feel like you're grinding through the same content. You feel like you're slowly becoming part of this world.

And then there's the gameplay.

Every run feels like its own little adventure. The randomness keeps things fresh, and the weapons are so incredibly unique that switching between them genuinely changes the way you approach a run. The different weapon aspects add even more variety, and the sheer number of boons you can acquire and combine to create some absolutely ridiculous builds is just *chef's kiss*. There's something incredibly satisfying about finding a combination that works perfectly and watching everything fall into place.

But what I appreciate the most is how seamlessly everything comes together. The gameplay, the writing, the progression, the characters, the music, the art style. Nothing feels like it's there just to fill space. Even failure feels like progress, and that's something I absolutely adore about this game.

While I have finished the main story, I still have things left to discover, builds to experiment with, and reasons to keep coming back. And that's probably the biggest compliment I can give a game like this.

Supergiant Games absolutely nailed it.

11/10. Absolutely loving it. If you're even remotely interested in roguelikes, do yourself a favour and play this game.

review:
I guess I would recommend this game but I'm personally very mixed on it.

While the art, world building, voice acting and characters are all great, I find the story and gameplay to be lackluster. Especially for a rogue lite. It lacks variety, so runs become stale pretty quickly, and while most rogue likes could be beaten on your first run with a lot of luck, Hades is not designed to be beaten on your first run.

The story is praised a lot, too, but from what I've seen it's pretty barebones. There's some world-building and lore you can find, but the main plot is pretty boring. I found myself skipping through dialogue in the lobby because it took too long and only 10% of the time was there new information.

I find the game to be a bit clunkily executed, especially if you're a rogue-like veteran. So my judgment is this: If you love rogue likes, don't bother with this one, it'll lack variety for you and become stale quickly. But if you want to get into rogue likes then this is the perfect entry point for you, and probably why this game entered the mainstream in the first place.

review:
(This review contains minor mechanical spoilers, and mentions minor details about the sequel at the end)

Hades is one of the few games I always enjoy returning to, even after having completed the full story several times. The incredible attention to detail and unique style present in every aspect of the game have always impressed me, from the first time I played.

The story is extremely well-written, immersive, and impactful. I was hooked to it and eager to progress it all the way through, and have started up a new save file to experience it again several times over the years. Progress feels meaningful and personal. More than any other game I have played, the world feels developed and alive. Characters have depth and respond to the things the player does, sometimes in the funniest and most unexpected ways. After over 200 hours of gameplay, I still encounter dialogues I haven't seen before.

I greatly enjoy the combat system. It's simple but also has a high ceiling to develop your skill, and there is lots of room for personal preference. There are many mechanics which exist to provide variety to the builds you can make and incentives for exploring that variety, but also freedom to play the way you want to. There is room to choose how difficult you want the game to be— whether more casual to experience the story, or more challenging to push your limits. Players who enjoy challenges can utilize some optional mechanics that increase the difficulty in creative ways which push you to make use of everything you can, and be rewarded for doing so. Unlike many games, it's not just artificial difficulty either, there is genuinely unique content to enjoy in doing so (i.e. not just numbers going up, which is part of it, but also interesting twists and enemies gaining new attacks & abilities).

There is also SO much content and replayability. Outside of the main story, there are so many other things you can choose to explore and progress, including side storylines, customizations, challenges, additional worldbuilding, and more. It doesn't feel like a chore, either— you can work on many things at once by just playing the game. Completionists can have a field day trying to max everything out if they so please. And, since the dungeons are randomized and there are so many build choices, no two runs feel the same. You are compelled to improve your adaptability and be ready for anything. At the same time, I would say the RNG is well-balanced, and there are systems you can unlock to greatly mitigate build-based RNG once you start finding ones you like to go for.

Overall, I would say Hades deserves all the awards and nominations it's received and more, and I can easily recommend it to a variety of players. You can tell the developers put the utmost of their efforts and passion into making it. I love the art style and original music so much I've used screenshots as my desktop background and listen to the music outside of the game. With Hades 2 out now, there's even more to look forward to afterwards. I would highly recommend playing the original first, as while Hades 2 has its own story, it builds on the story from the first game and has lots of fun references.

unlike many games, it's not just artificial difficulty either, there is genuinely unique content to enjoy in doing so (i.e. not just numbers going up, which is part of it, but also interesting twists and enemies gaining new attacks & abilities). there is also so much content and replayability. outside of the main story, there are so many other things you can choose to explore and progress, including side storylines, customizations, challenges, additional worldbuilding, and more. it doesn't feel like a chore, either— you can work on many things at once by just playing the game. completionists can have a field day trying to max everything out if they so please. and, since the dungeons are randomized and there are so many build choices, no two runs feel the same. you are compelled to improve your adaptability and be ready for anything. at the same time, i would say the rng is well-balanced, and there are systems you can unlock to greatly mitigate build-based rng once you start finding ones you like to go for. overall, i would say hades deserves all the awards and nominations it's received and more, and i can easily recommend it to a variety of players. you can tell the developers put the utmost of their efforts and passion into making it. i love the art style and original music so much i've used screenshots as my desktop background and listen to the music outside of the game. with hades 2 out now, there's even more to look forward to afterwards. i would highly recommend playing the original first, as while hades 2 has its own story, it builds on the story from the first game and has lots of fun references.

review:
《哈迪斯》是我玩过最上头的肉鸽游戏，没有之一。
先说战斗：手感太丝滑了，冲刺、普攻、投弹衔接流畅，配合奥林匹斯众神的祝福系统，每局都能组出完全不同的Build——有时候是无脑暴击流，有时候是弹射投弹流，玩几十个小时都不腻。
在说剧情：这个游戏最妙的地方，是把“死亡重来”做成了叙事的一部分。每次战败回到冥府大厅，都能跟角色们聊天，慢慢解锁扎格列欧斯寻找母亲的故事线。你越是死，越能了解这个世界，这种设计真的绝。
美术和音乐也是顶级水准，手绘风格独特，冥界的氛围感拉满，BOSS战的配乐燃到不行。
唯一的小缺点是后期重复挑战可能有点单调，但整体瑕不掩瑜。独立游戏天花板，没玩过的强烈推荐！

美术和音乐是我觉得哈迪斯里面挑不出毛病的，虽然我也不知道这种美术风格叫什么但是看着很漂亮的（希腊众神有些立绘角度看着非常像亚裔尤其赫尔墨斯，为了这个美术风格来玩的话也不算亏
还有就是文本量，哈迪斯的很多剧情都在对战里或者是死后，就我死了非常多次每次重来人物对话基本不重复，文本剧情量还是很大的，量大管饱
关于战斗，个人推荐用手柄比键鼠舒服很多简直手柄模拟器来的。然后就是局内战斗，对于手残来说不开神力模式真是难打的来，而且只要死一次就要从头再来，当时死在三头犬那里离老爹就一门之隔直接从头再来简直是抓心挠肝难受得要死（）只能说死后不重复的剧情让重新来也没那么无聊。还有就是祝福，随机性很高，打完一层没拿到想要的祝福概率不低，而且使用的武器强度和祝福有很大关联拿不到就很难受。除了上述之外如果你还能忍受反复打同一个流程的话，那这个游戏还是很好玩的，前期就是会死很多次来提升，等逐渐适应节奏弄清流程就好打得多，实在打不过就开神力也没什么的，选自己舒服的武器配合祝福中期打的还是很开心的

review:
从价格上来看是很合适的，但是从口碑来看是过誉的。
 说实话，我玩咩咩邪教都比玩哈迪斯过程要爽快。有以下4点巨无比严重的问题，影响游戏体验：
1.局外养成对局内影响太小/需要时间太长。成长主要靠玩家练习+爆肝。
2.不同武器之间上下限差距太大，肉鸽流程看脸导致很难养成完美体系。
3.爬塔设计导致前期关卡反复打，十分无聊乏味。
4.不同流派之间基本没有什么互动，完全不肉鸽。

实在不懂在父王前面放个畜生组合（看了一眼steam上打完这个组合成就也就一半左右这科学吗？）。导致打到父亲前面经常血量不足以至于纯靠多死几次才能摸清招数。即便摸清招数了，也经常没roll到好的组合打得十分难受。挑战了父王5把没过（中间还有好几把重开和没打到底，因为没有roll到好的buff），局外养成最大影响就重生次数，前面三姐妹和九头蛇都打吐了，打后面双人组，有的时候还被反杀。我是真的不想再刷武器了，真的。
然后这个弓箭是人用的吗谁设计的太拉了。真正的弓箭怕不是长矛吧吧？
还有我就是刷不出自己想要流派的门，怎么办呢？半路转其他流派可不可以呢？是可以的，但是之前的被动buff就没用了。因为这些流派之间都是各管各的，搞笑的是有的二合一buff还不如合并前好用。这能算是肉鸽吗我去。
被人盛赞的对话繁多，一个是对于国人来说不了解神话体系，还有个是我他妈被丝血反杀了，我还有兴趣听你那逼逼？有的一局玩下来连个紫buff都没有，真的红温了。还有那个吃血给buff的，加个30%多的普攻伤害，要你何用啊？还吃我25血？？？都已经是卖血了Buff的基础下限能不能给给高点。刷个10局的卖血可能也就出个一两个蓝buff，紫buff都没见过。
整体游玩体验比起爽快，更多是糟心啊。宁可给隔壁教徒铲屎去。

游戏是好游戏，玩的还行，想完整体验迎回冥后剧情也就大概20多把到30多把。但是我不能接受在雅典娜身上套用的政治正确，我讨厌政治正确，也绝不吃这一套。假如是你就是想在游戏里加入黑人女性角色，你明明有更好的选择，比如灶火女神赫斯提亚，黑夜女神赫卡忒等等。

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
补：啊....爬热度的感受，一把游戏成与败太过于依赖赐福，然后赐福又高度依赖于石榴，石榴花和蜜露提供的随机升级还有石榴的三选一升级如果一直抬不到你想要的赐福 这把就 直 接 寄。然后没有SL，中途选择放弃等于保留这局的种子，然后零资源结算。上一把玩的阿尔忒弥斯平a机枪，开局拿的普攻赐福，带石榴花，蜜露随即升级，结果打哈迪斯的时候一共七个赐福，然后普攻才三级，我吃柠檬，哈哈哈哈哈哈破防了，你这真是随机吗？

review:
受不了漫长的局外养成，非常非常肝。局内关卡又少的可怜，每个地区关底boss算作一关的话，才4关，新鲜感很快就过了。初始武器也不是满血武器，6把武器4个形态5个等级，都需要刷一遍4个boss。每把武器刷过一遍boss后同等难度就不给材料，得升级难度才能继续拿材料。
光武器就这样肝了。还有粗略感觉20个左右角色好感，角色属性，局内功能，隐藏地图（我看好像就一张）都需要一大堆杂七杂八的收集道具解锁
现在20小时每把武器初始形态都不能升满体验完，角色属性还有没解锁的，局内功能还是残缺，隐藏地图的材料都拿去解锁能优化局内体验的功能去了，也没解锁。
一看到还有这么多东西要靠反复刷解锁，大剑二形态也就改了个模型，改了出伤方式，动作模组根本没变。你要是改个动作模组，给点炫酷特效，我也就咬咬牙继续肝了，结果就这？一点继续玩下去的动力都没了。说白了就这点内容的游戏，撑不起这么肝的局外养成。

review:
I am FAR away from being the most knowledgeable person when it come to this series but I do earnestly think this is a very, VERY fun traditional base building rts game.

While I have yet to play a PVP match or any of the campaigns, I have gotten over 30 hours of playtime from "skirmish" and "comp stomp" matches alone in a little over 2 weeks.
Things I particularly like about AoE2DE at the moment include the way the game structures its factions, the soundtrack of the game and some specific factions I have grown to like (Namely The Sicilians and Hindustanis).

On the other hand, things I dislike about the game largely include things that can be chalked up to skill-issues(Feeling stressed from having a bunch of enemies in your base, having your invasion force killed off easily, etc). I will also note that -> from what I've seen <-, getting all the faction adding DLCs so that you have everything at your disposal for ranked play is a fairly expensive endeavor.

In conclusion, I really like this game and I will try to remember to update my review of it after I get some hands on experience with the PVP (Maybe including some ranked 1v1's) and campaigns of this game.

game: Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition
review:
I would like to preface this by saying I love Age of Empires 2. It's my favorite RTS, and one of the best games of all time. The Definitive Edition is arguably the best way to play it

That said, I hate how fragile the multiplayer is. It's not possible to re-join a game. This affects team games the most because if a player drops, their team will likely lose

This was acceptable in 1999 - friends were playing via LAN. If someone dropped, they could use the "restore game" function

It doesn't work in 2026 - strangers are playing via modern matchmaking, if someone drops, they just continue playing

It takes one disconnect to lose a 3 hour team game. It doesn't help that the game is prone to crashes

As far as I understand DE is based on the original code from 1999. The developers did a great job modernizing most parts. But the multiplayer is just not up to modern standards

PS: please fix shift queuing walls

game: Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition
review:
I am reviewing this from a strictly single player perspective, please keep that in mind.
That being said, I do not recommend this game for someone seeking a good single player RTS.
- The AI can outpace that player at every step of the way.
The first few missions in the first starter campaign are fine, but as soon as you step out of that one the AI is suddenly that same thing 90% of RTS are that focus more on single player. 
- "Rush the player" constantly is such an over used tactic for weak AI. You can't sit back and enjoy getting your civilization up and running because the enemy AI just keeps attacking, attacking, attacking and soon you find yourself spending 80% of your time defending yourself, repairing damage then trying to get back to setting up a farm.  I don't see how this is enjoyable from a single player perspective.
- Even if you focus on defense from the start, you are still running against the clock of "how soon will the enemy send an annoying force that I have to prepare for.
- I get this a "war" based game, but when a human being has to jungle 30 different things at once when the AI can do the same thing in 0.5 seconds it because a game of frustration rather than strategy or tactics.
- The only tactic that works at is to focus purely on military and quickly overwhelm the enemy with a massive force. How is that "strategy" when it's just "how fast can you click".

I know I'm going to be the odd man out on my review, and that's fine, but there are some of us who love the setting and the idea of bringing up your civilization AND having military conflict, but this game seems to only care about the military part and all the other stuff is just window dressing.

And before someone yells at me "this game is for multiplayer, yeah I get that, but it is sold and listened as single player as well, why bother with single player campaigns then?

Functionally the game runs great, looks good and is pretty bug free, gameplay wise, it's just not enjoyable.

game: Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition
review:
Look. I know pointing to my playtime and walking away is lazy, but like...what more do you want from me? It's the 1999 classic in all its glory but with a support level on par with any modern game. You can reasonably criticize the idea to upend certain long-standing gameplay systems with more recent patches and expansions, but at its core it still hits all the nostalgia notes while also allowing the growth that comes from 25+ years of game and map design evolution. And some of the newer, longer story campaigns from Chronicles or the recent Viking Sagas show that the underlying engine can power vastly different ideas than whatever was envisioned back then.

Like, I can play a complicated, 12-hour scenario full of triggers and conditions, with all the polish of a major studio, but I can also still play basically the same scenarios I played on my Pentium III when I was 15. Or I can just comp-stomp and vibe to the soundtrack. More than any of the other Definitive Editions, it's a platform for both memories and modern development.

时隔二十余年，《帝国时代 2：决定版》把无数玩家记忆里的经典 RTS 重新带回桌面。在 Steam 上保持着**特别好评**，它不是简单的高清换皮，而是在完整保留原版灵魂的基础上，完成了一次现代化重制。如果你是老玩家，这是重温青春最好的载体；如果你是新玩家，这是体验传统即时战略的教科书。
本作最大的亮点，就是原汁原味的核心玩法丝毫未变。黑暗时代、封建时代、城堡时代、帝王时代的升级节奏，采集资源、发展经济、扩张版图、集结军队的循环，依旧有着无与伦比的魅力。钟声一响，村民躲进城镇中心，这种刻在老玩家骨子里的紧张感完整保留。游戏内置数十个文明，每个文明拥有独特的单位、科技与加成，蒙古擅长骑射突袭、法兰克骑兵强势、不列颠长弓手远近闻名。不同文明的打法差异巨大，无论是防守运营还是快攻骚扰，都能找到适合自己的思路，重复游玩性极强。
画面上，决定版升级到 4K 高清画质，建筑、单位、地形全部重新绘制，光影、水面、植被细节大幅提升，同时保留原版美术风格，不会产生违和感。配乐也进行重录，熟悉的 BGM 经过重新编曲，氛围感拉满。战役内容极其丰富，从成吉思汗、圣女贞德到帖木儿，大量历史战役关卡，讲述不同文明的兴衰故事，新增的合作战役更是一大惊喜，可以和好友并肩完成历史剧本。内置场景编辑器与完整 MOD 支持，社区玩家自制的海量地图、战役、模组极大拓展游戏内容，让游戏的上限远高于本体。
但经典的底子，也带来一些无法回避的老问题。作为古早 RTS 的重制版，单位寻路依旧偶有拉胯，大量部队移动时容易出现卡堆、绕路的情况，在激烈对战中很容易影响战局。联机方面，服务器偶尔不稳定，匹配、掉线问题长期被玩家诟病；天梯环境里，炸鱼、消极游戏的情况时有发生，对新手不太友好。部分 DLC 内容质量参差不齐，新增文明与战役的口碑褒贬不一。操作逻辑源于老游戏，UI 设计偏传统，上手门槛偏高，新手很容易顾此失彼，一边管不住村民，一边被对手偷袭，需要大量对局练习才能入门。
它并不适合追求爽快、轻量化游戏的玩家。帝国时代 2 讲究经济运营、资源分配、侦查博弈，一场对局动辄几十分钟，需要耐心和专注力。但如果你愿意沉下心学习，会感受到 RTS 独有的成就感：从寥寥几个村民，一步步建立繁华城镇，组建大军击溃对手。
总而言之，《帝国时代 2：决定版》是 RTS 活化石。它带着老游戏固有的缺陷，却拥有难以替代的策略深度。老玩家可以回来重温情怀，新玩家如果想感受正统即时战略的魅力，它值得入手。有好友一起联机打战役、打对抗，体验会再上一个台阶。只要你能接受它古老机制带来的瑕疵，这便是一款可以玩上千小时的策略佳作。

I know we all hate super hand-holdy games but this goes so far in the opposite direction it's not even fun. There are many unintuitive mechanics/design choices that your only real option to understand how to play is to watch some videos on how to play. Incredibly lazy decisions made by the developer, I would not buy this game at regular price or even half price. It's also quite a hostile experience trying to play with a controller, so don't even bother. I'm sure it'll get better but everything feels so stiff and clunky - this is not a game that feels good to play, maybe it feels good to overcome... I'm getting a refund though and maybe I'll give it another go if it dips below $5.

I'm glad I caught myself before the 2 hour refund limit because some of the other reviews speak to issues that I wouldn't discover unless going much deeper into the game. If the controls weren't stiff and clunky, and they took 10 minutes to explain the basic mechanics of managing your raft (my first game I went to check out an island, my raft floated away, resources in the water despawned when my raft left, and I didn't have enough resources to build a new one, didn't know things could only be built on the raft, etc ,etc.)

It's also far to easy too die and far too punishing when you do, so the game itself doesn't even encourage learning how to play by playing. Maybe it's more fun if you have 4 people to gather resources, stab boars, and manage a single raft - but for me this was just 2 hours of my life wasted and filled with frustration.

I like the concept of this survival game. Building your raft into a mobile base/ floating factory that you take with you thoughout your journey, upgrading it along the way from story location to the next one.

Despite the graphics not being the greatest, it does not stop me from enjoying exploring above and under water.

The game lacks a bit in tutorials. In the beginning it is difficult to know what you exactly need to do, requiring watching Youtube and reading the wiki to get started. But once I picked up the basics, the game become much more enjoyable to play. 
Another thing that is a bit annoying is the low durability of most equipment, requiring you to replace it along the way quite frequently or to have a spare one ready whenever you are exploring a large island.

review:
While not the most glamorous of games, this is still a recommendation from me, as the survival system is engrossing enough to keep exploring just about until the end of the story.

It's relatively easy to just stick to the story to get through it as quick as one would like. But I'd posit anyone trying Raft out, to try and explore the game as more of a checklist - I know, sounds riveting. But the ideas are nice, and it's never all that difficult to posit a frustrated response either. And definitely play it with friends. It's not quite the full jank of atmospheres, but the comedic atmosphere and general whimsical nature of the game is to be enjoyed when exacerbated by someone laughing in your ear.

It's a nice ride. And a polished one at that. Don't expect to remember much of the story details after, but if you're fishing for a few nice evenings with friends, I very much recommend giving this a shot.

review:
Very unique take on the survival game genre, but really overshadowed by tedious and boring game mechanics. We found the game to be more fun when abusing its glitches and bugs.

Everything I will be describing came from a multiplayer session with my friend. I don't have much experience regarding singleplayer.

The first few hours of raft are extremely tedious. Sometimes a run can end because the game decides, that no resources will drift your way when you badly need them. 

The normal loot collection loop is insanely tedious and boring. The shark non-stop being on your ass doesn't make it more fun. The game expects you to collect an absolutely ridiculous amount of wood, plastic and metal. Planting trees on your raft barely speeds it up and collecting them by hand nets barely anything to work with. Plastic only drifts into your raft and metal, scrap etc come from gathering next to islands. Don't even get me started on the processing times for some of the materials via the Smelter. Many of the games mechanics artificially inflate your game time for no real reason.

Weapon durability being low and no repair station make this even worse, since you have to always craft a completely fresh set of tools if they break.

Gathering animals is insanely tedious. We beat the entire story without finding a single llama, because they just didn't spawn. Meanwhile, we had like 6 chickens and a goat.

Equipment breaks really quick, to the point where it might not even be worth crafting. I expect the same with armor (we never crafted it). The bow has a learning curve behind it, but even after using it for 20 hours it still felt bad, especially against any flying enemy.

To circumvent the absolutely tedious general gameplay loop, we starting dupping items via an exploit with saving and loading a backup. Problem is, that even with the huge amounts of resources, we didn't have enough for what we wanted to do/basic tools + basic infrastructure. I have no idea how the game expects you to collect so much wood, plastic, metal, scrap and titanium, when some recipes already take a large amount of it and that's just to craft said thing once.

The game's story consists of random scattered notes and a few locations. It's just kinda there and not really super interesting. You could probably "beat" the game in less than 5 hours if you really tried. The story mostly serves to give you tools to survive better and move to the next story location. Some of the puzzles were fun / interesting, but a lot of the time it's very straightforward. Some where just "go here, find this, then come back". Those were not very fun.

There are definitely a lot of bugs in multiplayer at least. A big one we encountered was, that the advanced controls caused the advanced anchor to be in a superposition. It was lowered for me, but not for the other player, causing the raft to glitch out. Some other meaningful ones I can mention are: completely negating fall damage, climbing walls vertically etc.

Overall, the game expects you to put in a ridiculous amount of time gathering simple resources and doing the same thing over and over again (gathering treasure for example). Don't even get me started on the achievement list. It has to be one of the worst ones I've ever seen in a video game, nothing but do this x50 times for no real reason. No fun. The idea behind the game is good, but the execution of game mechanics really drags down the entire experience. I'm sure some people could enjoy a really slow paced survival game that takes real hours and that offers doing stuff over and over again. But I don't think tedious game mechanics and wasting your time for no reason is fun or engaging.

review:
A beautiful and scenic game that is undercut and overwritten by BEES. want to hear the wash of the waves, the call of seagulls, the creak of wood, and the putter of old engines? sorry, all you get is BEES. for some reason BEES were made to be the cornerstone of all mid-late game progression and their sound radius is so loud and so wide it spoils much of the ambiance of the game in solo play. 

A pleasantly simple and elegant crafting system in which you use a few metal ingots to craft a nice upgrade to your wooden spear. the progression feels smooth and rewarding with just the right amount of granularity and you better have an autoclicker because you need to click precisely 120 times to fill the recycler to make money for the trader. you need to fill it 8-10 times to get enough money to by the various valuable and vital things from the trader. it takes 7 clicks to plant and harvest a crop that feeds you for 8 minutes, 7 more to cook it, plus more clicks to add wood, more clicks to manage inventory, even more clicks and inventory juggling to make more complex foods. refilling your water bottle once is five clicks. everything is clicks. a few things have auto-act when you hold down the key or click, but most things do not.

it's a fun experience with friends, a peaceful experience playing solo, and the game overwrites all of your backup saves if you die, forcing you to use its respawn mechanic which deletes all your inventory because fuck you. this is fine early on but lategame it gets incredibly grindy. in the final chapter of the game there's an area completely underwater. you need oxygen tanks. multiple of them. each one takes 30-40 clicks to make and a bunch of time spent managing the smelters. plus multiple sets of flippers each of which takes another 20+ clicks to make. some of the traps in that part of the game instant kill you from full health with full armor on, and the game deletes all of those items and overwrites all your saves.
